passages.happening:
‘Then the LORD sent Nathan to David’ (verse 1). Nathan tells the king a case. “There were two men in a certain city, one rich and the other poor” (verse 1). The rich man had great flocks and herds. ‘But the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb that he had bought’ (verse 3). He raised it with his children. ‘It shared his food and drank from his cup; it slept in his arms and was like a daughter to him’ (verse 3).

A traveler comes to the rich man. Instead of taking an animal from his own flocks to feed his guest, ‘he took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for his guest’ (verse 4).

David burns with anger: “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die! Because he has done this thing and has shown no pity, he must pay for the lamb four times over” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
The chapter before ended with the narrator's verdict, that what David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD. Now God acts on it. The king whom no human court could reach is judged by the word of God, spoken through a prophet.

Nathan's story works because it comes to David as a judge. The king was Israel's last court of appeal, and a poor man wronged by a powerful neighbor was exactly the kind of case he was meant to hear. Hospitality required a host to feed a traveler, which is why the rich man needed an animal. The detail that the lamb was like a daughter to him makes the theft unbearable.

The story is a trap in the form of a legal case. David hears about someone else, gives his verdict, and is about to find that he has sentenced himself. His sentence mixes outrage with law. The law of Moses required fourfold repayment for a stolen sheep that had been killed.

Prophets in Israel had a remarkable role: they could confront kings in God's name. Other courts of the ancient Near East had prophets too, as texts from the city of Mari on the Euphrates show, but they rarely condemned their king so directly for a crime against one of his own people.
passages.later:
The law David applies is in Exodus: ‘he must repay five oxen for an ox and four sheep for a sheep’ (Exodus 22:1).

A later prophet would face a later king over a close cousin of this crime. When Ahab took Naboth's vineyard after Naboth was killed, Elijah brought him the LORD's question: ‘Have you not murdered a man and seized his land?’ (1 Kings 21:19).
passages.asks: David saw the rich man's sin at once and could not see his own. Ask whether there is a fault you condemn quickly in others that you have never named in yourself. And ask who in your life is free to tell you the truth.

passages.happening:
“You are that man!” (verse 7). Then Nathan gives the word of the LORD. God anointed David king and delivered him from Saul; he gave him his master's house and the kingdom of Israel and Judah, and he would have given more. ‘Why then have you despised the command of the LORD by doing evil in His sight?’ (verse 9). David struck down Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites and took his wife.

So ‘the sword will never depart from your house’ (verse 10). God will raise up trouble against David from his own house, and his wives will be taken and given to another in broad daylight: ‘You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel’ (verse 12).

Then David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against the LORD.” “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have shown utter contempt for the word of the LORD, the son born to you will surely die” (verses 13-14).
passages.hearers:
Four words turn David's whole story. ‘You are that man’ catches the king in his own verdict.

The word of the LORD that follows first rehearses God's generosity. He anointed David, delivered him, gave him his master's house and kingdom, and would have given more. Only then does it name the sin. And the judgments mirror the crime. David used the sword, so the sword will not leave his house. He took another man's wife in secret, so his own wives will be taken in broad daylight. These words become the outline of the chapters to come.

David's confession is two words in Hebrew, and Nathan's pardon is almost as short. There are no excuses. He does not blame Bathsheba or Joab. When Samuel confronted Saul, Saul made excuses (1 Samuel 15). David owns his sin before God. The verb for taken away means to make something pass over, to carry it off from the one who bore it.

The chapter holds two things together that run through the rest of the book. David is forgiven, and he does not die. Yet forgiveness does not erase every consequence. It refuses both cheap grace and endless condemnation.
passages.later: Psalm 51, which its heading ties to this moment, gives the longer prayer: “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight, so that You may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge” (Psalm 51:4). Paul quotes those words in Romans 3:4: when a sinner confesses, God is shown to be in the right.
passages.asks: David said, ‘I have sinned against the LORD’, and did not add a word in his own defense. Ask what it would cost you to confess something without a single but. And ask whether you believe that God takes sin away when it is confessed.

passages.t: The child dies, and Solomon is born
passages.happening:
‘After Nathan had gone home, the LORD struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became ill’ (verse 15). David pleads with God for the boy. He fasts, and spends the nights lying on the ground in sackcloth. He will not get up or eat with the elders of his household.

‘On the seventh day the child died’ (verse 18). David's servants are afraid to tell him. When he sees them whispering, he asks, “Is the child dead?” “He is dead,” they replied (verse 19).

Then David gets up from the ground, washes, puts on fresh clothes, goes into the house of the LORD and worships, and afterward he eats. His servants cannot understand it. He answers that while the child was alive he fasted and wept, hoping the LORD might be gracious and let him live. ‘But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me’ (verse 23).

David comforts his wife Bathsheba, and she gives birth to a son, and they name him Solomon. ‘Now the LORD loved the child’ (verse 24), and he sends word through Nathan to name him Jedidiah, ‘because the LORD loved him’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Fasting, lying on the ground and wearing sackcloth, coarse cloth of goat hair, were signs of grief and of pleading with God. Normally they came after a death, not before it. David reverses the order. He pleads while the child lives, and when the child has died he washes, worships and eats. His servants are bewildered, and his answer is one of the most quoted passages in the chapter.

His hope while the boy lived rested on one word: the LORD might be gracious. To be gracious is to show favor that is not earned. David had no right to the child's life. He had only God's freedom to give.

The text says that David comforted Bathsheba. She has lost her husband, and now her son.

Then the LORD loves the next child. Jedidiah means beloved of the LORD. Solomon is the son through whom the promise of chapter 7 will continue.
passages.later:
Psalm 127, the one Song of Ascents headed as Solomon's, uses the word yedid, beloved, which sounds like Jedidiah: ‘for He gives sleep to His beloved’ (Psalm 127:2).

Matthew's family tree keeps the whole story in one line: ‘David was the father of Solomon by Uriah’s wife’ (Matthew 1:6). Many years later, at Nathan's urging, Bathsheba would go to the aged David, and he would swear to her that Solomon would reign after him (1 Kings 1:30).
passages.hard:
Why should an innocent child die for his father's sin?

This is one of the hardest lines in Samuel, and the text does not soften it. Some things can be said without explaining it away. The law of Moses forbade human courts to put children to death for their fathers' crimes (Deuteronomy 24:16), so the text is not describing human justice. It speaks of God as the giver and taker of life. The Old Testament often shows the sins of leaders falling on their households, a reality of human life as much as a sentence from God. Some interpreters read the death as sparing the child a life marked from birth by adultery and murder; others think that is speculation.

David's words in verse 23, ‘I will go to him, but he will not return to me’, have been read as hope of meeting again after death, and many Christians have drawn comfort from them for children who die young. Others take them to mean only that David too will go to the grave.

What the chapter does not do is call the child's death good. It shows David grieving, pleading, and at last worshiping a God he cannot fully understand.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: David pleaded with God while there was hope, and worshiped when the answer was no. Ask how you pray when you do not know what God will do. And ask whether there is a grief you have carried in silence that you could bring to God and to someone you trust.

passages.happening:
Meanwhile Joab fights against Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and captures the royal fortress and the city's water supply. He sends for David: ‘Now, therefore, assemble the rest of the troops, lay siege to the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me’ (verse 28).

So David gathers the army and takes the city. He takes the crown from the head of their king, a talent of gold set with precious stones, and it is placed on David's head, and he carries off great plunder (verses 29-30). He puts the people of the city to work with saws, iron picks and axes, and at the brick kilns, and he does the same in all the Ammonite towns. Then he and the army return to Jerusalem (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The siege of Rabbah began in chapter 11. It ends here, though it probably ended well before Solomon's birth, since a long siege would hardly outlast two pregnancies. The account is placed here to close the story of the war that framed David's sin.

Joab takes the water supply and then calls the king, so that the king and not the general gets the credit for the city. The crown weighed a talent, perhaps thirty kilograms or more, which suggests it may have belonged to a statue. The Hebrew word for their king, malkam, is very close to Milcom, the name of the Ammonite god, and the Greek translation and several modern versions read it that way.
passages.later:
Chronicles tells the capture of Rabbah in almost the same words (1 Chronicles 20:1-3), though it tells nothing of Bathsheba or Uriah: ‘Then David took the crown from the head of their king’ (1 Chronicles 20:2).

Forced labor appears again under Solomon, who ‘conscripted these people to be forced laborers, as they are to this day’ (1 Kings 9:21).
passages.hard:
What did David do to the people of the Ammonite towns?

Verse 31 has been read in two ways. Older translations took it as the torture of prisoners with saws and brick kilns. Most modern translations, the BSB among them, understand it as forced labor: the people were put to work with saws, picks and axes, and at the kilns.

Even on the gentler reading, forced labor is a wrong in itself, and the text does not hold it up as a model. The chapter that tells of David's forgiveness ends with his power over others still on display.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Joab handed David the honor of a victory Joab had won. Ask whether you are quick to take credit that belongs to others. And ask what it would look like to make sure the people who did the work are seen.
